hook: Cornell University engineers built a microscopic fiber forest that keeps electronics 17°C cooler.

sections.voiceover: Cornell University engineers built a microscopic fiber forest that keeps electronics 17°C cooler.
sections.visual_cue: Close-up microscopic shot of Zylon fibers in a forest-like arrangement.

sections.voiceover: Researchers packed Zylon nanofibers into epoxy matrices to create this new cooling structure. How does this forest outperform standard commercial thermal pads?
sections.visual_cue: Animation showing fibers being packed into a grid structure.
b_roll: Animation of Zylon fiber alignment in epoxy

sections.voiceover: Except this design achieves a thermal conductivity of 16.8 watts per meter-kelvin.
sections.visual_cue: Text graphic displaying the conductivity value clearly.
b_roll: Digital readout of 16.8 watts per meter-kelvin

sections.voiceover: The team tested their creation on a surface running at 1.2 watts of power. This advancement provides a powerful new solution for cooling modern electronics.
sections.visual_cue: Side by side visual comparison of heat maps.
b_roll: Heat map comparison of thermal pad vs fiber forest

sections.voiceover: The fibers successfully dropped the temperature by exactly 17°C.
sections.visual_cue: Close up of the fiber forest hardware.
b_roll: Macro shot of Zylon polymer structure
